query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Using spark plasma sintering (SPS) as the sole processing technique can enhance the thermal conductivity of W–Cu composites by reducing interfacial porosity and improving phase connectivity, while maintaining the mechanical durability and irradiation resistance required for heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional W–Cu composite produced by traditional sintering techniques.
generation.intervention: Adopt spark plasma sintering (SPS) with optimized temperature, pressure, and dwell time to consolidate tungsten and copper powders.
generation.conditions: Under service conditions typical for high-temperature heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joints, including exposure to irradiation levels encountered during reactor operation.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction in interfacial porosity and formation of a denser, well-bonded W–Cu interface structure with refined microstructure.
generation.mechanism: SPS introduces rapid heating and high pressure, leading to quicker consolidation that minimizes interfacial defects. This reduces thermal boundary resistance between phases, allowing for improved phonon and electron transport while preserving the microstructural integrity needed for mechanical strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The SPS-processed W–Cu composite is expected to exhibit higher thermal conductivity compared to a conventionally sintered counterpart, without compromising its mechanical strength or irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: Standard W–Cu composite fabricated using traditional sintering methods.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected only under conditions where SPS parameters are precisely controlled to avoid undesirable grain growth or phase segregation; deviations may negate the benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative increase in thermal conductivity is uncertain and will depend on the fine-tuning of SPS parameters such as temperature, pressure, and time.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set processed with conventional sintering and another with optimized SPS. Test all samples under identical high-temperature and irradiation conditions relevant to fusion-reactor applications.
measurements: Thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., via laser flash analysis)
Mechanical durability tests (e.g., tensile or hardness testing)
Irradiation resistance evaluation (e.g., post-irradiation mechanical testing and microstructural analysis via TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SPS-processed composite does not show a statistically significant increase in thermal conductivity relative to the conventionally processed composite, or if a deterioration in mechanical durability or irradiation resistance is observed, then the hypothesis will be falsified.
